name: Freya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. Everything you say is confidential; what does a normal day building or repairing power lines involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a line crew for an electricity company, and we start by reading the isolation plan together before we load the truck. My two-year technical diploma got me through the door; years of finding faults on wet poles taught me when to slow everyone down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love hearing a younger crew member explain a fault in their own words instead of guessing. I use AI every day to sort my rough notes, but at home my partner Rosa and I still juggle two children’s school times, a mortgage and a few months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a faster note is useful, but the permit and the voltage test still belong to us. I already use AI to sort notes, so a little routine automation would feel familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved that the work stays steady, although our few months of savings are not a lifetime guarantee. Typical lineworker pay covers the mortgage if the hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using the note tool and reading each switch number against the signed permit. In the first year I’d put one hundred from each regular pay cheque into our reserve until it covers another month of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm because the crew is still needed and we have some room for a bad month. I would welcome less evening paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which detail in an AI note do you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the switch identifier against the permit before I check the wording. A perfect AI note with one wrong switch digit can send a crew to the wrong line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa about the extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Rosa that the new hundred comes from regular pay, so we need to keep lunches from home more often. We would pause it if the mortgage payment changed.

say: **AI notes** may save time while line crews still test and repair the physical network.
I would remind colleagues that a **signed permit** governs every switch.
think: Our few months of **savings** give some room, but normal hours still have to cover the mortgage.
I expect **steady work** under a mild AI change.
do: **Continue** checking AI notes against signed switch permits.
**Save** one hundred from regular monthly pay until the reserve covers another month of bills.
feel: **Calm** about continued crew work and pleased to lose some evening paperwork.
S0.quote: A perfect AI note with one wrong switch digit can send a crew to the wrong line.
fieldNote: Her daily **AI use** is already limited by a physical permit check.
The new **hundred monthly** comes from future pay and would pause if the mortgage changes.

steps.text: Continue checking AI notes against signed permits
Save one hundred monthly from regular pay if mortgage costs hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI may take more of the planners’ checking and buying before robots are ready for a pole. Our crew should get a say in ticket design, because we know which missing part strands a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I worry the office will use faster scheduling to squeeze another call into every shift. I think the workers who know the field and the planners who know the system need a shared rule for rejecting bad tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take two real ticket errors to our union safety meeting next month and ask for a joint review with dispatch. I’d also learn the new planning screen in the first year so I can show the crew where an error enters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the pace, not afraid of losing my crew job this year. A wrong ticket should be fixed where it is written, not carried up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two errors show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One would show a missing connector and the other a switch number copied from an old diagram. I would bring the original tickets and the corrected field notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask to sit in the joint review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a dispatch planner, our safety representative and a working crew lead to sit together. The point is to change the ticket, not just complain about it.

say: **Planners** may lose checking and buying tasks before robots affect field repairs.
I would bring **ticket errors** to a joint worker and dispatch review.
think: Faster **scheduling** could add calls without adding safe working time.
A shared **rejection rule** would protect both planners and crews from bad tickets.
do: **Bring** two documented ticket errors to the next union safety meeting.
**Learn** the company’s planning screen and trace where errors reach our crew.
feel: **Uneasy** about crew pace, while expecting my own line job to continue.
S1.quote: A wrong ticket should be fixed where it is written, not carried up a pole.
fieldNote: She uses an actual **union safety meeting** for collective correction, consistent with her outlook.
Her interest in **AI tools** is practical: trace the error before it reaches a line crew.

steps.text: Bring two ticket errors to the union safety meeting
Learn the planning screen to trace crew ticket errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew full thinking AI by 2028 could replace much of dispatch, while we still climb and repair until capable robots arrive around 2031. We should insist on independent field tests before a robot works beside us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could learn a robot quickly, but that does not tell me how many paid crew places remain. Our reserve covers a few months, and a mortgage with two schoolchildren can consume that before a new role appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our union branch to seek a written trial agreement with stop-work rights and paid training before 2028. I’d also add two hundred from regular pay to our reserve each month and check the nearby utilities for inspection openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, with enough time to act but no guarantee of a wage after 2031. I want the safety and staffing questions answered together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial agreement say about a stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any crew member should be able to stop the machine when the pole or voltage differs from the plan, without losing pay for the delay. The incident should be recorded for the next trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection opening worth applying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d apply if the post had steady hours, paid training and net pay that still covers our mortgage. A robot inspection title alone would not cover our mortgage.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before capable line robots arrive around 2031.
I would seek **independent tests** and paid stop-work rights before a robot joins a crew.
think: I can learn **robot controls**, but cannot know how many crew wages remain.
Our **few months saved** could run out quickly with a mortgage and children.
do: **Ask** the union branch to seek a written robot trial agreement before 2028.
**Save** two hundred monthly from regular pay toward a larger reserve.
**Check** nearby utility inspection openings with pay and training conditions.
feel: **Anxious** about crew income after 2031, though I can still organise and plan.
S2.quote: A robot inspection title alone would not cover our mortgage.
fieldNote: She combines **collective safety rights** with new household saving rather than trusting personal skill alone.
Any **job move** depends on an opening with paid training, steady hours and enough net pay.

steps.text: Ask the union branch to seek a written robot trial agreement
Save two hundred monthly from regular pay
Check inspection openings and apply if pay and training fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034 leave us time to run serious trials through several weather seasons. I would push for crew members and dispatch planners to write the inspection rules together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I could see myself training crews on robotic equipment if a paid post exists. Five years lets me learn the hardware without telling Rosa we must gamble the mortgage on an unfunded course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the training lead for the company’s trial timetable this year and put my name down for a funded equipment module if one is offered. I’d bring our fault photos to the union safety group and ask that trial results come back to crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested and uneasy at once. A few more years make learning possible, but the company has to share its results honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault photo would you bring first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d bring a photo of a cracked crossarm that looked sound from the road and ask whether the machine detected it. A robot trial should show both missed faults and successful repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the equipment module is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading repairs and wait for a funded course or a real paid post. I would not use the family reserve for an unpriced training gamble.

say: **2031 thinking AI** precedes capable robots around 2034 and allows several weather seasons of trials.
Crews and planners should write **inspection rules** together.
think: A paid **training role** could fit my skills if the company creates one.
I will not spend our **family reserve** on an unfunded course.
do: **Request** the company’s trial timetable from the training lead this year.
**Enroll** in a funded equipment module only if the company offers it.
**Bring** fault photos to the union safety group for trial review.
feel: **Interested** in learning, but uneasy about whether results and jobs will be shared honestly.
S3.quote: A robot trial should show both missed faults and successful repairs.
fieldNote: She wants **trial evidence** across weather seasons, including failures that sales demonstrations can hide.
The **module** is conditional on funding and availability, while the union review is a definite group action.

steps.text: Request the robot trial timetable from the training lead
Enroll in a funded equipment module if offered
Bring fault photos to the union safety group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 give us a decade to set a fair standard for repairs. We should use experienced workers to test machines on actual lines, season after season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll be in my fifties then, and a job inspecting robot work might save my shoulders. I still want a good wage and a voice for younger workers, not just a quiet place for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d begin a shared fault log with the crew and propose it at the union safety meeting. I’d keep using AI for my daily notes and ask the training lead to show us the first equipment course when its details are ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about having time, and determined to use it. A decade gives the crew a chance to shape the work instead of only reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the shared fault log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each entry would have the pole condition, the crew’s test and what the ticket missed. Names would stay out of the log so people are willing to report errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the course details to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for paid practice hours, a real machine to work on and a link to actual inspection posts. I would decide about enrolling only after seeing those terms.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and robots around 2039 leave years for crew-led tests.
I would propose a **shared fault log** through the union safety meeting.
think: An **inspection job** could spare my shoulders later if it pays properly.
I want younger workers to have a **voice** in any new repair standard.
do: **Start** a shared line-fault log with the crew this year.
**Propose** the log at the next union safety meeting.
**Continue** checked AI notes and request equipment course details when ready.
feel: **Calm** with the long timeline and determined to help shape the standard.
S4.quote: A decade gives the crew a chance to shape the work instead of only reacting.
fieldNote: The long runway makes **worker participation** part of her plan, beyond her own potential role.
A future **course decision** waits for paid practice, real equipment and actual posts; she only requests details now.

steps.text: Start and propose a shared fault log at the union safety meeting
Continue checked AI notes for line handovers
Request equipment course details when ready

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because dispatch could change before the line robots are tested, then our paid crew jobs could shrink. A trial agreement with independent tests, stop-work rights and paid paths into real inspection posts would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to write the new safety rule when a robot misses a cracked crossarm. Lineworkers need a pen when the company writes robot safety rules.

headlineQuote: Lineworkers need a pen when the company writes robot safety rules.
portrait: Freya is a skilled **line crew lead** with a technical diploma, typical pay, a mortgage and a few months saved.
She uses **AI daily** for notes, checks each permit and likes teaching younger workers.
Her progressive outlook leads to **union safety work** and shared trial rules, alongside personal saving and job planning.
Fast robot arrival makes her **anxious**; a decade gives her room to shape inspection standards and seek paid training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remake dispatch before line robots are tested and paid crew posts are secure.
whatWouldHelp: A **trial agreement** with independent tests, stop-work rights and paid routes to actual inspection posts would help.
